segments.text: Today's subject is how retail investors can approach exposure to private companies like SpaceX
and the mechanics of evaluating any future initial public offering.
I'm not a licensed financial advisor and this isn't financial advice.
Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security.
Always do your own research before putting real money to work.
SpaceX has no announced IPO yet the mechanics of how retail investors actually access or
approach any future listing are worth mastering now. SpaceX continues to operate as a private company
with a valuation shaped by tender offers rather than public markets.
Yet the question of how ordinary investors might one day participate remains relevant.
This episode examines the current state of SpaceX exposure options alongside the broader reusable
process for evaluating any IPO. By the end listeners will understand the realistic paths available
today and carry a discipline checklist for assessing newly public companies in either Canadian or US
accounts. SpaceX was founded in 2002 and has grown into a major private aerospace firm
whose Starlink satellite constellation now generates the majority of its revenue through broadband
services while the core launch business supplies launch capacity and government contracts.
The company has raised successive rounds of private capital and conducted periodic tender offers
that allow existing shareholders to sell shares to new investors at negotiated prices.
These tenders have produced reported valuations in the range of $200 billion or higher in recent years
though exact figures fluctuate with each transaction and remain non-public.
Elon Musk has repeatedly stated a preference for keeping the company private
to avoid quarterly reporting pressures and short-term market demands.
No formal IPO registration or pricing has been announced as of late May 2026,
making any discussion of a public listing speculative. Retail investors therefore face two distinct
questions. How to gain any exposure while the firm stays private and how to approach an
eventual public offering if one occurs? The second question applies far beyond SpaceX
and forms the reusable framework that occupies the second half of this episode.
Traditional IPOs involve a company filing an S1 registration statement with the SEC,
selecting underwriters who market the shares through a road show,
and ultimately pricing the offering after collecting indications of interest from institutional buyers.
The first day pop often occurs because the offering price is set conservatively to ensure
the deal clears, leaving room for immediate trading gains once public supply and demand take over.
Direct listings bypass the underwritten allocation process and allow existing shares to trade
immediately on an exchange, while SPACs reverse merge a private company into a publicly traded shell,
each route carrying different costs, timelines, and allocation outcomes for retail participants.
Retail investors rarely receive meaningful allocations at the IPO price because underwriters prioritize
large institutions. Most individuals must buy in the open market after trading begins,
frequently at a premium to the initial offering price. Post IPO lockup agreements typically prevent
insiders and early investors from selling for 180 days, after which a wave of supply can pressure
the stock if those holders choose to exit. The S1 itself contains the prospectus that details revenue
recognition policies, customer concentration, capital structure, dilution from convertible securities
or options, and the use of proceeds. Disciplined readers focus on these sections rather than the
summary marketing language. Historical studies of IPO cohorts show that on average, newly public
companies have underperformed broad market indices over the subsequent one to three years,
with the effect most pronounced among firms at price at peak valuation multiples or operate in
crowded sectors. Canadian investors face the additional layer of currency conversion and the choice
between TFSA, RRSP, or taxable accounts, each carrying different tax treatment for foreign dividends
and capital gains. Platforms that facilitate pre-IPO access, such as forged global or equity
zen, generally require accredited investor status and impose minimum investments that place them out
of reach for most retail participants. Funds or holding companies that carry basic stakes exist,
but often trade at premiums or discounts to net asset value and may carry their own liquidity
restrictions. Waiting for a public listing, if one materializes, therefore remains the most
straightforward route for the majority of individual investors. A disciplined investor begins by
confirming whether any IPO candidate meets basic criteria of revenue visibility, a credible path
to sustained free cash flow, and a share structure that limits excessive dilution.
Before committing capital, the same investor reviews the S1 for related party transactions.
Insider ownership percentages and the size of the lock up overhang relative to daily trading volume.
Account selection follows. A TFSA or RRSP may suit longer term Canadian holdings where
contribution room exists, while a taxable account offers loss harvesting flexibility if the position
is held only briefly. Retail platforms such as interactive brokers, quest trade or wealth simple
allow post IPO purchases in either CAD or USD, yet none provide allocation at the offering price.
The investor then asks whether the current valuation already prices in optimistic growth assumptions
and whether comparable public companies trade at materially lower multiples.
Common mistakes include chasing the first day pop without reviewing lock up expiration dates,
ignoring currency risk on US listed names, or treating an IPO as inherently different from any
other equity purchase. The framework generalizes, apply the same revenue quality and dilution screens
to every newly public company, regardless of sector or headline appeal, and consider a waiting
period of several quarters to observe post lock up trading behavior and earnings delivery.
This approach treats IPOs as one subset of equity opportunities rather than a distinct asset class
requiring special rules. The strongest bull case for any high profile listing rests on the
possibility that early revenue traction and technological leadership translate into durable
market share. Yet historical base rates show many such companies later face margin compression
or competitive response once public scrutiny increases. The bear case highlights the documented
tendency of IPOs to underperform in the years after listing, driven by both initial overoptimism
and the eventual release of locked up shares. Private market platforms carry their own frictions,
accreditation requirements, high minimums, wide bid-ask spreads, and the risk that the platform itself
faces liquidity or regulatory issues all come into play. Even if SpaceX eventually lists,
the timing, pricing, and lock up terms remain unknown. So any current exposure through indirect
vehicles carries basis risk relative to a future public share price. Currency movements between
CAD and USD add another layer of volatility for Canadian investors holding US securities. None of
these considerations constitute a prediction. They simply illustrate that the range of outcomes
is wide and that past cohort performance offers only probabilistic guidance rather than certainty.
Rule 1. Treat any unannounced IPO as speculative and evaluate exposure roads on their actual
accessibility and cost rather than anticipated future liquidity. Rule 2. Read the S1 for revenue
concentration, dilution mechanics, and lock up size before considering any post IPO purchase.
Rule 3. Default to waiting several quarters after listing to observe trading behavior
once insiders can sell. Rule 4. Apply the same account type and position sizing discipline
used for any equity, recognizing that IPOs carry no special exemption from ordinary market risk.
Watch for the next concrete filing of an S1 by a company with meaningful private market visibility.
That document will provide the first verifiable data set on which to test the framework.
The show returns to its regular daily markets coverage next episode. Thanks for listening to modern
investing techniques. This episode used AI voice synthesis of my voice. Editorial selection and analysis
are my own.
